title: The Confluence
subtitle: Hierarchical Clustering · hclust + cutree + summarise
story: You came down into the red canyon to map its springs, and the flood season came early. Sheltering, you find a stair into a drowned hall the old makers left behind — their floodworks, a single sealed tunnel that climbs to safety, an engraved panel no living hand has set, and a map of the whole canyon with every height left blank. A ladder climbs from the hall to the high springs. The makers built this place to be run by someone who could read the canyon as they did — its waters sorted into families, its channels into one branching tree. Climb, and roam the whole canyon: read the springs at each junction to learn which waters are kin, and mark each junction's height on your map as you pass it. Then come back down to the hall and read the shape of the land itself — before the water climbs to meet you.

done.title: The map lied
done.body: The carved map grouped the springs by the fork they rise in — but two springs' water swore a different kin, and you saw it. The storm breaks; the canyon fills. Kinship hides beneath the surface, and only the reading finds it. Back down to the hall — the panel is waiting, and your map of heights is full.

escapeDone.title: Free of the canyon
escapeDone.body: You draw the waterline across your map and count the canyon's severed limbs — and the panel takes it. You throw the great wheel; a sluice grinds, the flood turns aside, and the sealed tunnel opens. You climb as the hall drowns behind you, into rain and open sky. The canyon kept its one promise: read me truly, and go free.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: The whole canyon was one skill in disguise: sorting many things into a nested tree of families by how alike they are. Each junction taught one move of hierarchical clustering, and the escape was the move made physical — reading the true branching structure of the land and cutting it into groups.
